content.overview: Vicarious liability makes one person answerable for the tort of another because of a relationship (typically employer-employee) and a connection between the tort and the relationship (course of employment). It is not a substitute for proving the underlying tort of the wrongdoer.

sections.heading: Employer and employee
sections.body: Identify a contract of service (control and integration tests as guides). The tort must occur in the course of employment — authorised acts and wrongful modes of doing authorised acts may attract liability; a frolic of one's own may not.

sections.heading: Independent contractors
sections.body: Ordinarily the employer is not vicariously liable for an independent contractor, subject to non-delegable duties and hazardous operations exceptions.

sections.heading: Track B
sections.body: Plead the employee's tort and the employment nexus. Join employer and employee where appropriate. Evidence: appointment, duties, time and place of the act, and benefit to the employer's enterprise.

enhancement.definition: Vicarious liability is liability imposed on one person for a tort committed by another because of a legally recognised relationship, most commonly employer and employee acting in the course of employment.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The relationship alone is insufficient; the tort must be sufficiently connected with authorised work or the course of employment.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Indian tort law is largely uncodified. The governing rules are developed through common-law principles, Indian judicial decisions and applicable legislation for particular fields.
essentialIngredients: Act within course/scope of employment where employer liability is alleged

Confirmed: bus owner/transport operator held vicariously liable for the operational negligence of the driver acting in the course of employment.

Confirmed: criminal acquittal of the driver under Section 304A IPC does not bar or dismiss civil suit/claim in tort; culpable rashness under criminal law requires a more drastic standard than negligence sufficient to establish tortious liability.
Confirmed: doctrine of res ipsa loquitur applied to draw an initial presumption of negligence where vehicle struck an overhead electric cable, rejecting the defence of Act of God.

Statutory/procedural framework: uncodified common law received under Article 372; motor vehicle accident claims adjudicated under specialized statutory framework (Motor Vehicles Act) before MACT or civil court under Section 9 CPC.

distinctions.title: Vicarious liability differs from personal negligence
distinctions.left: Vicarious liability: derivative liability imposed on the employer for an employee's tort committed in the course of employment.
distinctions.right: Direct negligence: primary liability arising from the employer's own failure to take reasonable care (e.g. incompetent staff, unsafe equipment).

rows.left: Derivative / secondary liability for another's wrongful act
rows.right: Primary liability for breach of employer's own personal duty

rows.left: Proof that employee committed tort in course of employment
rows.right: Proof of employer's personal fault or direct omission

distinctions.title: An employee's merely private frolic is generally distinguished from an act sufficiently connected with employment.
distinctions.left: Course of employment: authorized act or unauthorized mode of performing authorized work; employer remains liable.
distinctions.right: Frolic of one's own: independent venture wholly unconnected with employment duties; employer is exonerated.

rows.left: Act is closely connected with authorized employment tasks
rows.right: Act is a total departure on an independent personal purpose
Employer escapes liability; primary tortfeasor alone is liable

caseLaw.name: N. K. V. Bros (P) Ltd. v. M. Karumai Ammal
caseLaw.holding: Judgment dated 21/03/1980. The Supreme Court upheld the finding that the transport operator/bus owner was vicariously liable for the rashness and negligence of its driver acting in the course of employment when the vehicle struck an overhead high-tension wire. The Court ruled that an acquittal in a criminal case does not bar civil liability under the law of torts, as criminal culpable rashness under Section 304A IPC is more drastic than the civil standard of negligence, and applied res ipsa loquitur.
caseLaw.relevance: Direct Supreme Court authority establishing employer/owner vicarious liability for employee negligence in the course of employment and confirming that criminal acquittal does not defeat civil tort claims.
